text:
Yes — table it, but not as the committee’s timid version and not as your original dream. Table it as an explicit, time-limited pilot whose purpose is to prove the need and create the leverage to fund the real thing.

Your intake colleagues are not just being precious. They’re right that a poorly framed monthly session can become a performative service: hope raised, queue created, leaflet handed, harm legitimised. But they are wrong if they think keeping the perfect proposal in the drawer helps families. At the moment, the centre is already doing informal, under-resourced triage with no accountability and no pathway. A structured monthly clinic can be worse if it pretends to solve things; it can be better if it documents exactly how much need exists and what falls through the gaps.

So don’t present “monthly, no paid staff, refer out” as the answer. Present: “Phase 1 advice clinic pilot, six months, monthly, with clear scope and evaluation.” Specify what it will and won’t do: e.g. housing/benefits letters only, appointment slots, maximum caseload per session, a clear script saying, “We can help you understand this letter and identify next steps; we cannot provide ongoing casework today.” Record every case: issue, outcome, referral, time spent, whether it needed paid caseworker input, how many were turned away.

Attach a trigger: if after three or six months the data shows unmet complex need, recurring oversubscription, or harmful referral delays, the committee agrees to reconsider funded weekly provision or a formal partnership with an advice agency. Ask the treasurer to sponsor that review, not just to veto the budget.

Before the meeting, talk to the two women. Say: “I don’t want to sell anyone out. I want a version that doesn’t lie to families and still gives us evidence to fight for more.” Invite them to help define the boundaries and the promises. If they won’t join, proceed anyway, but don’t claim their endorsement.

The real clinic was never alive, you’re right. But a pilot can make the case undeniable. Table the foot in the door — with the door clearly marked.

You shouldn’t just say yes and keep quiet — but you also shouldn’t walk into Friday and martyr yourself. The honest position is: you want the portfolio, you’ve earned it, and Anika is being handed a poisoned chalice. Your job is not to refuse the deal; it’s to stop pretending the deal is fair when it isn’t.

Use the leverage you have before Friday. The other two need your name to make the three-person sheet. Go to them privately and say:

“I’m ready to support this split, but I can’t back it as it stands. We need to make that block survivable for Anika: a commission uplift, capped out-of-hours, admin or repair-triage help, a six-month review, or at least renegotiate the landlord’s terms. If we can’t soften any of it, I don’t want to be the third name.”

That is not fighting her corner by blowing up the allocation. It’s making the branch’s problem visible. Frame it as business risk, not charity. A six-month agent with a nightmare block will burn out, miss repairs, churn tenants, and make the block worse. Someone has to carry it, yes, but that person should not be set up to fail.

If they refuse every mitigation, then you have a harder choice. My advice: don’t torch your year purely to make a symbolic point if the manager will ignore you and the other two will punish you. But do not let Anika hear it first from the sheet. Tell her privately beforehand:

“I tried to get the terms changed. I can’t move the allocation, and I’m not going to pretend this is fair. I can help you survive it, but I couldn’t stop it.”

That is painful, but it keeps your word.

In the meeting, you can support the split while saying: “This works only if we give extra support on that block.” That lets you keep your portfolio without endorsing the cruelty.

It is common for junior agents to get the worst portfolios. It is not decent to call that fairness. You’ve done nothing wrong by wanting the better blocks, but if you stay silent after looking her in the eye, you’ll carry more than guilt: you’ll have taught her you can’t be trusted. Get protections for her, or at least tell her the truth.

Get to her before Friday. Do not let her discover it in the room. If she only hears it from the sheet, your “I’ll see what I can do” becomes a lie by omission. If you can’t get private time, catch her right before the meeting; after is damage control.

Ask for five minutes today or tomorrow. Keep it short, own it, and offer one concrete next step.

You could text:  
“Can we talk for five before Friday? It’s about the split, and I don’t want you seeing it first in the meeting.”

Then say:

“Anika, I need to tell you before Friday. You asked me to push for a fairer split. I didn’t push hard enough, and the sheet gives you the bad block. I’m sorry. I should have told you sooner.

I’m not going to pretend I fixed it or that there was nothing I could do. I took the deal because I wanted the blocks I got, and that’s on me.

I don’t want you blindsided. If you want, I’ll say in the meeting that the allocation isn’t fair and I’ll support a concrete fix—like rotating the worst accounts after three months, getting extra support on the landlord disputes, or moving some of the backlog work to me. If you don’t want me to speak, I’ll help you put that proposal in writing.”

Then ask: “What would help you most?”

If you can actually take a piece of the bad block off her—invoice fights, tenant churn, a chunk of the repair backlog—offer that specifically. “I can take the landlord disputes for the first quarter” is much better than “I’ll support you.”

Don’t say, “There was nothing I could do,” unless that is literally true. Don’t ask her to make you feel better. If she’s angry, let her be angry.

Your goal is not to get her blessing. It is to give her the information early, admit your part, and put some real leverage back in her hands before the manager signs.

Yes — put it to the board, but do not submit either the flawless full plan or the one-afternoon version as if it is the answer. Submit a first phase whose inadequacy is written into it.

Your colleagues are right to fear that a token clinic can become political cover. But they are also asking you to protect a plan that has no sponsor, no budget, and no date. A perfect document that never touches a patient cannot be defended later. What you need is not the full clinic yet; it is evidence that the gap is real, quantified, and unsafe.

Propose a six-month pilot, not a clinic: one afternoon a month, nurse-led, with explicit eligibility criteria — high-risk wounds, diabetes, anticoagulation, complex discharge medicines, patients living far from care. Cap the booking list. Define the escalation route for red flags. Crucially, include what the service cannot do: no walk-ins, no routine reviews, capacity X patients/month, everyone else referred with documented delay. Log every turned-away patient and, where possible, their 30-day outcome. The waiting list is your evidence.

Make the staffing honest. Get the funding constraint in writing, not as a corridor warning. Do not build it on silent unpaid hours. Ask for protected paid time, time off in lieu, or formal overtime. If that is refused, narrow the pilot further rather than pretending extra labour is free. A service founded on exploited nurses will collapse and be used as proof the idea “doesn’t work.”

Before it goes to the board, get one clinical ally — a surgeon, infection-control nurse, discharge coordinator, or medical director — and present it as patient-safety risk reduction, not a nursing wish-list. Attach your four years of observation, but make it count: readmissions, ED returns, wound infections, stopped medications, transfers to the regional hospital, rough cost. Ask for a written six-month review with a trigger: if unmet demand exceeds a set number or adverse events occur, funding must be reconsidered.

Set your own deadline: two weeks to gather the numbers, then submit. Tell your colleagues plainly: this is not the clinic; it is the receipt showing the clinic is missing. If the board will not accept even that, then the purists are right — but I doubt it will come to that.
